Live-Queryable RDF Data Dumps with Apache Parquet

papers.abstract: Knowledge graph completion requires models to use both textual descriptions and relational structure. Existing LLM-based methods either encode KG structure as discrete tokens or refine a restricted set of candidate entities, and these two directions have largely been studied separately. We propose CoSC for LLM-based KGC, which combines discrete structural coding with similar entity information. Specifically, an LLM generates an initial candidate entity ranking from discrete structural codes, after which information from entities with structures similar to that of the query entity refines the ranking. Experiments on FB15k-237 show that CoSC outperforms existing baselines on MRR and Hits@10 while remaining competitive on Hits@1.
papers.title: LLM-Based Knowledge Graph Completion Combining Discrete Structural Coding with Similar Entity Information
LLM-Enhanced Beyond-Equivalence Ontology Matching with Scope Definitions and NLI Verification
MARITA: Mining Approximate Rules in Tables
Multi-Layer Knowledge Graph Construction for Cybersecurity Vulnerability Analysis

papers.abstract: Ontologies are widely used to represent and organize complex knowledge in domains such as biomedicine and healthcare. However, constructing reliable ontologies remains challenging, as class hierarchies, whether manually or automatically constructed, may contain subtle subsumption errors that require careful refinement. We study this problem in CASTON, a casting-domain ontology, and present a lightweight but scalable refinement workflow that combines a fine-tuned ontology embedding model with Large Language Models (LLMs). The embedding model is used to extract a limited number of candidate axioms for refinement together with possible replacement candidates, and an LLM then returns repair suggestions. In a small expert evaluation, the default configuration using a CASTON-fine-tuned OnT embedding model and Qwen3-8B produced reliable high-confidence repairs: all six high-confidence replacements were accepted by both domain experts. The implementation is available at https://github.com/HuiYang1997/OntRefine.
papers.title: Ontology Refinement with Embeddings and LLMs: A Case Study on CASTON
PROTON-QA 1.0: A Nucleus for Provenance-Aware Ontology-Grounded Nuclear QA Benchmark

Reasoning over Hybrid Graphs: Adaptive Causal Path Discovery for Reliable Knowledge Graph RAG
Reconstructing Wikidata Statement Lifecycles for Temporal Maintenance Analysis
RossijskijFeatrDB: Modeling Russian Imperial Opera Sources as Linked Data

papers.abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) excel at representation learning on Knowledge Graphs (KGs), achieving stateof-the-art performance on tasks like link prediction or entity classification. However, their high computational complexity, inherent to their user-defined message passing (MP) algorithm, still prohibits their widespread adoption, especially for large KGs. Current efforts to mitigate the scalability bottlenecks of GNNs on KGs, such as subgraph sampling, are often task- and model-specific, and do not reliably guarantee lossless (if applicable) runtime/space reductions. To address this, we extend Relational Sparse Matrix Multiplication (RSPMM), originally designed to losslessly lower the space complexity of composition-based MP with pointwise composition functions, to support more expressive functions (e.g., 2x2 block-diagonal matrix multiplication, Givens rotation, circular correlation). Our method delivers significant task-independent reductions in runtime and space for current GNNs on KGs and facilitates efficient re-implementations of GNNs that maintain near state-of-the-art performance on challenging KG tasks, for a fraction of computational costs.
papers.title: Scalable GNN-based Knowledge Graph Representation Learning with Efficient Message Passing
Symbolic Routing for Executable SHACL Repair: What Can Be Automated Safely?
Towards A Provenance Framework for Modelling Human Oversight of AI Decision Making
Towards an evaluation framework for event-centric knowledge graphs
Unravel-RDF: A Developer-Oriented Query Abstraction for Interactive RDF Knowledge Graph Web Applications
What Drives Schema Capture in Link Prediction?

papers.abstract: SNAP-KG is a framework for assigning newly arriving entities to semantic communities in a growing knowledge graph (KG) using only their raw features, with no graph access and no retraining at inference time. It was evaluated on five multi-view benchmarks and a 2.4M-node OGB-WikiKG2 KG. In each of these datasets, at least one graph view is homophilous, meaning that connected nodes usually belong to the same class, and SNAP-KG performs well on all of them. This paper asks what happens outside that setting. We extend the evaluation to three heterophilous graphs (Texas, Wisconsin, Chameleon) and measure the edge homophily of every view. When no homophilous view is available, clustering quality drops sharply for both SNAP-KG and the transductive baselines used in its original evaluation. What decides this is the homophily of the relation, not the number of relations. Multi-view fusion still helps, but only when at least one homophilous relation provides a reliable foundation. The homophily assumption is therefore shared by the whole method family, not specific to SNAP-KG. We argue that heterophilous multi-view clustering is a separate research problem, outside the scope of this work. As future work, we outline how a heterophily-aware teacher could be distilled into SNAP-KG's projector to serve both homophilous and heterophilous KGs.
papers.title: When Connected Does Not Mean Similar: Charting the Homophily Boundary of SNAP-KG for Streaming Entity Integration

papers.abstract: Despite the critical role of grey literature in scholarly communication, artefacts such as Calls for Papers (CfPs) remain largely isolated from modern Scholarly Knowledge Graphs. The unstructured and highly heterogeneous nature of these documents has traditionally hindered their large-scale processing. In this demo paper, we present the Conference Organisers and Content Identifier (COCI), an AI-based framework designed to extract fine-grained, structured metadata from raw CfP texts. COCI employs a multi-stage pipeline that combines Large Language Models (LLMs) with semantic mapping techniques to integrate extracted entities with established knowledge bases, including OpenAlex, DBLP, TIB ConfIDent, and the AIDA Dashboard. By disambiguating authors and semantically aligning topics and conference series, COCI bridges the gap between informal scholarly dissemination and structured Semantic Web resources, laying the foundation for systematic analysis of non-publisher-based academic events.
papers.title: COCI: Conference Organisers and Content Identifier
Demonstrating ProbSPARQL: Querying Knowledge Graphs with Multi-dimensional, Uncertain Numeric Data
Demonstrating the MLIPs Ontology: Querying Machine-Learning Interatomic Potential Metadata in SPARQL, Natural Language, and via MCP
Designing and Evaluating Knowledge Graph Pipelines with KGpipe Explorer

papers.abstract: Ontology documentation, visualization, and validation are usually carried out with separate tools. This split workflow slows down development and makes knowledge transfer harder. We present OntoInk, an open-source MkDocs plugin that brings these activities together. Within a single documentation-as-code pipeline, OntoInk renders interactive ontology diagrams, validates instance data against SHACL shapes, runs OWL\,DL reasoning, and supports inline Turtle editing. General-purpose diagram plugins for MkDocs cannot parse RDF, dereference IRIs, overlay SHACL constraints, or run OWL reasoning. Compared with standalone ontology visualization tools, OntoInk embeds interactive and editable diagrams directly into documentation pages. A live demo and source code are available at \url{https://ise-fizkarlsruhe.github.io/ontoink/}.
papers.title: OntoInk: Interactive Ontology Visualization, Validation, and Reasoning
OOPS!+: Improving Ontology Pitfall Detection with Large Language Models
ParliamentRAG: An Authority-Aware Multi-View RAG System for Italian Parliamentary Proceedings
PathExtractor: Extracting Path Information in Graph Databases (Demo Paper)
rdflib-endpoint: Exposing Idiomatic Python Functions as Federated SPARQL Services
REFV-KG Explorer: Causal and Stakeholder-Oriented Exploration of Renewable Energy Policy Discussions

papers.abstract: Trust and reputation systems underpin reliable interactions in large, distributed networks. However, conventional models typically propagate trust only forward, offering no accountability for endorsers regarding whom they vouch for, and leaving newly joined nodes without a meaningful initial reputation. RepuLink addresses these limitations by proposing a two-layer trust and reputation model that integrates direct interaction feedback with domain-specific endorsements. Crucially, it holds endorsers accountable via Backward Endorsement Penalty/Reward Propagation (BEPP/BERP). This paper demonstrates RepuLink-Tool, a deployable, full-stack reference implementation of this model. The application enables nodes to interact, rate, and endorse each other, while tracking reputation via a live dashboard and an interactive trust network graph. Furthermore, we introduce a new Linked Data layer built on top of the application. This layer features a lightweight OWL ontology encompassing nodes, interactions, ratings, endorsements, pairwise trust assessments, and computed reputation scores annotated with PROV-O provenance. It also provides an on-the-fly RDF projection of each user's trust network in multiple serialisations, alongside a scoped SPARQL endpoint that nodes can query live against their own data.
papers.title: RepuLink: A Linked Data Platform for Accountable Trust
RIGOR App: A Demo System for Retrieval-Augmented Generation of Ontologies from Relational Databases

papers.abstract: This poster presents SciKGDash, a production-ready dashboard designed to support human-in-the-loop curation and quality assurance in the Open Research Knowledge Graph (ORKG). The system addresses common challenges in crowdsourced research knowledge graphs, including duplicate predicates, missing semantic descriptions, incomplete metadata, and structural inconsistencies. By combining strategic monitoring, usage analytics, and operational curation workflows, SciKGDash enables curators to detect quality issues, analyze graph usage patterns, and carry out targeted improvement actions. The dashboard aims to support proactive quality governance, improve the reliability of machine-actionable research knowledge, and reduce the effort required for large-scale knowledge graph maintenance. Future developments focus on live quality scoring, automated recommendations, contribution tracking, and user-centered mechanisms to democratize knowledge graph curation in the ORKG. Poster presented at the ISWC 2026, Posters & Demo, Bari, Italy.
papers.title: SciKGDash: The Human-in-the-Loop Curation Dashboard for the Open Research Knowledge Graph
SHACL-Wizard: Guided Creation of SHACL Shapes

papers.abstract: We demonstrate X-DigCheck, a domain-independent environment for building and maintaining application profiles as they co-evolve with the data they describe. Profiles developed against a fixed ontology quickly drift from the schema they were meant to capture. X-DigCheck treats profile construction as a continuous ontology-data co-evolution loop: data are lifted into RDF against the profile, checked through competency questions and SHACL, and the resulting reports jointly drive revisions of the ontology, mappings, constraints, and graph. The loop is agnostic to the domain and to the pipeline that produces the graph. We validate and demonstrate the tool in the cultural heritage domain, on the construction of RupeMagna-RTI, the first Reflectance Transformation Imaging (RTI) specialisation of the Cultural Heritage Survey ODP (CHS-ODP), aligned with CIDOC-CRM/CRMdig, ArCo, CHAD-KG, and Getty AAT, with semRTI as the lifting pipeline of this use case. The demonstration lets visitors run one full turn of the loop -on the shipped Rupe Magna (Grosio, Italy) RTI survey, or on a profile and graph of their own -executing the competency-question and SHACL checks live and reading the bidirectional coverage report that flags modelling gaps and stale assumptions. The result is a portable co-evolution environment for profile engineering, together with a reusable RTI application profile produced through it. A screencast of the demonstration is available at https://zenodo.org/records/22210609.
papers.title: X-DigCheck: Co-Evolving Application Profiles and Knowledge Graphs, Demonstrated on the RTI Documentation of Rupe Magna
YAGO: A Logically Consistent Subset of Wikidata

papers.abstract: Scientific Knowledge Graphs (SKGs) rely on increasingly complex and heterogeneous semantic models, whose reuse and interoperability require ontologies and other semantic artefacts to be understandable by both machines and humans. However, existing ontology documentation tools provide limited support for modern reuse-oriented modelling practices, where entities are distributed across imported modules and enriched through cross-module annotations. This paper presents the new version of LODE, a re-engineered and extensible framework for generating human-readable documentation of semantic artefacts. LODE preserves the established single-page, W3C Recommendation-style documentation paradigm of its legacy predecessor, and introduces a modular architecture that separates artefact interpretation (Reader), internal representation (Model), and rendering (Viewer). Served as a web service, LODE supports the documentation of OWL ontologies and enables additional documentation features (e.g., entity stand-alone documentation, RDF entity provenance, Markdown rendering). We demonstrate the applicability of LODE through the documentation of the Scientific Knowledge Graph Interoperability Framework ontology (SKG-O), showing how it improves the accessibility and reuse of modular scientific knowledge graph models.
papers.title: Supporting the understanding of ontologies for scientific knowledge graphs with the new version of LODE

papers.abstract: Scholarly Knowledge Graphs (SKGs) support literature search, scientific discovery, and agent-assisted research. Yet, most approaches to SKG construction pre-specify the knowledge unit to be represented, typically named scholarly entities or contribution-level statements, and retain only the publication content expressible through that unit. This choice produces two dominant yet distinct paradigms: concept-centric SKGs that preserve entities and local relations, and statement-centric SKGs that capture high-level discourse in sentences. In both cases, the graph reflects a chosen extraction target rather than how a paper constructs and communicates knowledge. We introduce SUDO, the Scholarly Upper Discourse Ontology, which defines how knowledge elements are organized and related to form a paper’s research narrative, namely its scholarly discourse. Using linguistic principles that generalize across fields and tasks, SUDO enables each publication’s scholarly discourse to be constructed from the bottom up as a coherent, source-grounded representation. Applied consistently across papers, the same structure connects their research narratives into a global scholarly discourse without discarding local context or provenance. We demonstrate SUDO’s capabilities across a comprehensive suite of scholarly knowledge-modeling use cases and performance improvements on a downstream Large Language Model (LLM)-based scientific QA task.
papers.title: SUDO: From Scientific Publications to Global Scholarly Discourse

papers.abstract: GitHub README files contain information needed to discover and reuse scientific artifacts, yet much of it is absent from conventional scholarly metadata. Large language models (LLMs) can convert this heterogeneous content into structured metadata, but open-schema extraction is difficult to evaluate without document-level gold annotations and consistent field names. To address this challenge, we applied an agreement-based evaluation methodology for assessing open-schema metadata extraction without requiring document-level gold metadata. The methodology is applied to metadata independently generated by six representative LLMs from 200 README files in the NERdME corpus using a zero-shot, evidence-grounded prompt. Output well-formedness, extraction cardinality, field-name diversity, and agreement over fields, values, and field–value pairs are evaluated under exact and embedding-based semantic matching. JSON validity ranges from 0.990 to 1.000 and record completeness is at least 0.998, although extraction cardinality varies substantially across models. Semantic matching raises multi-model field–value Jaccard similarity from 0.0000 to 0.1053 and Krippendorff’s alpha from 0.1784 to 0.5237. Agreement differences between open- and closed-model groups are limited, whereas within-family agreement consistently exceeds cross-family agreement. These results show that models often extract semantically similar metadata while organizing it differently, demonstrating that inter-model agreement is a useful diagnostic for evaluating open-schema metadata extraction, although it is not a substitute for correctness validation.
papers.title: Open-Schema Metadata Extraction from GitHub READMEs: A Cross-Model Agreement Study

papers.abstract: Type specimen (insect individual) catalogs in entomology contain large amounts of biodiversity data, including changes and losses in species numbers. Yet these catalogs lack machine readability because they are published as journal articles without annotations. Therefore, to analyze and trace how type specimens have changed in either collections or the domain over years, they must be represented in a structured format. This work constructs a domain-specific schema from competency questions (CQs) from four user groups in the entomology domain and its library, leveraging Darwin Core terms where needed. We then apply collaborative large language model annotation to the type specimen catalogs using the domain-specific schema to construct a knowledge graph. Finally, we evaluate this knowledge graph using SPARQL queries for these CQs.
papers.title: Knowledge Graph Generation from Biodiversity Catalogs with LLM Annotation

papers.abstract: Model Cards were introduced in 2019 as a means to provide a human-readable, clear summarization of machine learning models, including key metadata such as license, biases or evaluation results. While the adoption of these cards has grown by the scientific community (being adopted by open platforms like HuggingFace) model cards are usually manually filled by authors when uploading their models, thus leading to missing or inaccurate information. Moreover, model cards are not semantically interoperable, since they are not compliant with any ontology or data model. This paper presents Paper2ModelCard (P2MC), a framework for end-to-end generation of model cards from research papers. P2MC integrates processing tools for correctly parsing the input PDF into a structured format (using existing tools like SciPDF and LightOnOCR-1B), which is then processed by an ensemble of models, each targeted towards efficiently extracting specific information from the input. The FAIR4ML ontology is used as the backbone to generate the model cards, in order to ensure their interoperability. Moreover, P2MC links the generated model cards to existing scientific knowledge graphs, such as SemOpenAlex or LinkedPapersWithCode. Demo: https://w3id.org/p2mc Code: https://github.com/oeg-upm/p2mc
papers.title: Paper2ModelCard: A framework for the automated generation of model cards from research papers
Retraction without Traction: Towards Handling Post-publication Invalidation in Open Science Infrastructure

papers.abstract: Understanding who researchers collaborate with, when and how their research groups form, and how these evolve over time is a foundational prerequisite for constructing multidimensional, evidence-based researcher fingerprints – a requirement that has become increasingly urgent in the context of ongoing reforms in research evaluation advocated by initiatives such as DORA, the Leiden Manifesto, and CoARA. In this paper, we propose an egocentric approach for fine-grained research group detection, operating at the scale of individual researchers’ ego networks, as extracted from Scientific Knowledge Graphs (SKGs), and requiring the ego node to be present in all identified research groups – a constraint that is not merely technical but reflects a commitment to researcher-centred analysis. Our approach builds on the Leiden algorithm as its computational core and is grounded in SKGs, which provide the heterogeneous, open scholarly metadata necessary to trace collaboration patterns at scale in a reproducible and transparent manner. We evaluate the proposed method through a user evaluation involving 10 researchers with diverse backgrounds and career stages, demonstrating its ability to surface meaningful and interpretable collaboration structures. The research groups identified constitute the structural scaffold upon which richer characterisations of scholarly identity – including roles, seniority, contribution types, and publication patterns – can be built in subsequent work, contributing to the broader goal of fairer and more transparent research assessment.
papers.title: From Data Footprints to Researcher Fingerprints: Temporal Ego-centric Research Group Detection in Scientific Knowledge Graphs

papers.abstract: The growing number of fraudulent publications poses a serious threat to scientific integrity; however, a substantial number of these publications remain undetected in the published literature. Irrelevant citations, among other integrity problems, is a prevalent concern in fraudulent papers. To help address this problem, we developed ReCitE (Reliable Citation Evaluation): a framework to identify fraudulent papers by analyzing citation relevance, that is, whether a reference actually supports the claim to which it is attached. The framework includes parsing a PDF, extracting references, finding the referenced papers in open bibliographic databases, then prompting a large language model to identify the claims tied to each citation, score their relevance, and provide a brief justification for each assessment. We manually evaluate the quality of citation context extraction and evaluate citation relevance with five open-weight, locally deployable LLMs on a public dataset of 22,381 labeled citations. The best-performing model for citation relevance was Gemma 2-27b, with an F1 score of 0.981 and an ROC AUC of 0.981, comparable to the state-of-the-art results based on SBERT embeddings. An error analysis shows that misclassifications occur due to generic citation contexts, uninformative abstracts and citations used to establish background rather than support a direct claim. This method is not intended to replace human reviewers, but rather to serve as an automated tool that helps reviewers, editors and integrity sleuths flag papers for closer inspection.
papers.title: ReCitE: Evaluating Citation Context Quality and Relevance with Large Language Models

papers.abstract: Scientific papers keep much of their quantitative content in tables and supplementary files, where a number means something only through its header, caption, unit, analytical method, and the conventions of its field. Recovering the rows and columns of a table is therefore not the same as recovering the scientific fact it reports. Most semantic table-interpretation methods assume that a clean table is already available and subsequently map its cells or columns to ontology terms, whereas most publication-level extraction systems are designed for a single domain. We study a middle path: a shared process that reads a paper and its supplementary files, gathers evidence from several parsers and a language model, and reconciles that evidence, while a bounded human-authored task module for each task supplies the domain meaning. The module lists the canonical names the graph may use, the surface forms that map to them, a small set of derivation rules and validity constraints, an identity key, and the bindings used to write RDF. It defines what a task is allowed to emit; it does not try to list every convention of a field. We build four such modules (for drug-discovery chemistry, materials science, machine learning, and mineral geochemistry) in the ArticleMiner framework, and evaluate them on 163 papers, including a new geochemistry benchmark with expert-curated ground truth. In comparisons against a same-LLM few-shot baseline, the point estimates favor ArticleMiner on all four tasks, with uncertainty on the two smaller benchmarks. The geochemistry comparison also includes access to supplementary files, so its improvement cannot be attributed to domain guidance alone.
papers.title: ArticleMiner: Ontology-Guided Knowledge Graph Construction from Scientific Publications

papers.abstract: Moving beyond the high-level metadata available in bibliographic databases is essential to achieve a richer, more accurate representation of research paper content. Current retrieval and evaluation frameworks rely heavily on basic structural attributes, which fail to capture the nature and intrinsic value of scholarly contributions. To this end, we propose a joint community effort with the workshop audience to collaboratively design and refine a dedicated Research Contribution Ontology. We believe establishing this domain-independent semantic model will provide new and better ways to retrieve content, and fundamentally transform scientific evaluation, supporting qualitative assessment frameworks that move beyond canonical, purely quantitative metrics. In this vision paper, we argue that the time is ripe for this evolution. With the rapid expansion of open-access literature, mature parsing software, and LLMs capable of structured extraction, we now possess both the data and technology. What is missing is the formal semantic representation to link these capabilities together. We present an initial core ontology outline as a concrete foundation for collective development and future integration into scholarly knowledge graphs.
papers.title: Research Contributions: Towards a Formal and Semantic Representation
SciGraphChat: Retrieval-Augmented Generation over Scientific Knowledge Graphs

papers.abstract: The exponential growth of scientific literature makes it extremely difficult for researchers to identify the most relevant prior work to cite at a given point in a manuscript. Local citation recommendation (LCR) addresses this problem by suggesting, for a given citation context, the papers that best support the underlying claim. Existing approaches to LCR are typically confined to single-stage retrieval, prefetch-then-rerank pipelines, or generative formulations that only weakly exploit the structural relationships between papers, authors, and citation contexts. In this paper, we propose a Scholarly Knowledge Graph (SKG)-based approach to LCR that jointly exploits the semantic structure of scholarly data and neural representation learning. We first construct ArgKG, a domain-specific SKG for the argumentation-theory literature, comprising 1,576 collected corpus papers, 24,438 additional referenced papers (26,014 in total), and 82,868 citation contexts, modelled as an RDF graph that reuses established scholarly ontologies and vocabularies to represent papers, authors, citation links, and citation-context semantics explicitly. Building on this representation, we introduce a two-tower architecture that learns a shared embedding space for citation contexts and candidate papers through contrastive learning. Candidate papers are represented by metapath-based features extracted from the SKG – their title and abstract, reference neighbourhood, and previously observed citation contexts – fused using a transformer-based encoder. We report experimental results across several feature-set and architecture configurations on ArgKG and on the established ACL-200 benchmark, showing that combining a paper’s own title and abstract with its citation neighbourhood yields the best-performing configuration and outperforms most of the existing LCR baselines on ACL-200. To support reproducibility, the code, trained models, and SKG construction pipeline are publicly released at https://github.com/Ba-aH/SciteKG.
papers.title: Local Citation Recommendation via Heterogeneous Graph Neural Networks and Contrastive Learning

papers.abstract: Research onemotional introspection in Large Language Models (LLMs) —understood functionally as causal informational coupling between a target model’s self-report and an independently measured emotion-related internal direction — remains an emerging empirical question within a broader literature on affective behaviour and internal representations. This definition concerns context-bound functional evidence, not direct inspection of activation tensors and is agnostic about consciousness or subjective experience.Findings are reported through heterogeneous terminology, model families, units of internal analysis, intervention techniques, evaluation protocols, and standards of causal evidence, and studies routinely conflate emotionally appropriate output, latent representation, causal influence, introspective access, and self-regulation, although these rest on fundamentally different levels of evidence. This position paper argues that progress here requires not only new experiments but a semantic representation and assessment framework for the evidence itself. We treat a structured review of the literature as adomain analysis, identifying the concepts, entities, relationships, and evidence types to be represented, and propose anEmotional Scientific Knowledge Graph (E-SKG): a provenance-aware, statementcentric graph of emotion constructs, internal model components, interventions, reported states, behavioural effects, experiments, datasets, evaluation methods, claims, and publications. Building on existing scientific knowledge graphs, our contribution is not an implementation but a research agenda: a conceptual semantic model, seven representation requirements, competency questions, and future directions. We use healthcare and surgical robotics as a high-stakes application case, while designing the E-SKG as domain-general infrastructure that can be extended to other emotion-dependent settings.
papers.title: Representing Evidence of Emotional Introspection in Large Language Models: A Scientific Knowledge Graph Research Agenda

papers.abstract: The CIDOC CRM family is not only a schema for museum collections. Its extensions formalise the apparatus through which research knowledge is produced and justified: CRMsci models scientific observation and measurement, CRMdig the provenance of digital processes, CRMinf inference and belief. Together they constitute a schema for research data, and the obstacle to their adoption is documentary rather than theoretical: four normative documents, four code conventions, and eighty-nine typed links crossing document boundaries. This paper presents the CIDOC CRM Periodic Table, a single-page browser rendering 131 classes and 480 property entries from CIDOC CRM 7.1.3, CRMsci 3.2, CRMdig 5.0 and CRMinf 1.2.1 as one navigable surface, with two inference facilities: a one-step triple builder admitting only the class–property combinations licensed by declared domains, ranges and the subclass closure, and a multi-step path finder enumerating property chains between two classes. Because all loaded models are merged into one code-keyed dictionary before the hierarchy closures are computed, both resolve chains that cross model boundaries; we document the addition of CRMsci and the three cross-model tests it made possible, and report preliminary uptake signals from 56 months of analytics, with the reading they support.
papers.title: The CIDOC CRM Periodic Table: Documentation You Can Test to Support the Adoption of Scientific Research Ontologies for the Humanities

sessions.description: Wikidata is an open knowledge base hosted by the Wikimedia Foundation that can be read and edited by both humans and machines. As the central repository for structured data used by Wikipedia, Wiktionary, Wikisource, and many other Wikimedia projects, Wikidata has become an essential resource for academic research and industrial applications, supporting data integration, semantic technologies, and knowledge-driven systems. Over the years, a growing body of research and practical innovation has highlighted Wikidata's role as a cornerstone of open structured knowledge. Previous editions of the Wikidata Workshop have addressed topics such as data quality, multilingual knowledge contributions, community dynamics, the evolution of collaborative knowledge graphs, and the interaction between Wikidata and emerging AI technologies. The 6th Wikidata Workshop at ISWC 2026 welcomes contributions covering the broad spectrum of research and applications related to Wikidata and collaborative knowledge graphs. We are particularly interested in recent developments in the Wikidata ecosystem, including new infrastructures and capabilities such as GraphQL-based query access, Wikidata partitioning and dataset extraction for large-scale experiments, and embedding-based representations that enable semantic search, machine learning, and downstream AI applications. We also encourage work exploring the role of Wikidata in the rapidly evolving Generative AI ecosystem, including AI agents, tool and skill integration, Model Context Protocol (MCP) interfaces, retrieval-augmented generation, and knowledge grounding. These directions highlight how collaborative knowledge graphs can provide reliable, structured context for intelligent systems. The workshop brings together researchers and practitioners from academia and industry to share ideas, present innovations, and discuss the future of open knowledge and AI-ready knowledge graphs.
sessions.organizers: Nicolas Ferranti, Marcelo de Oliveira Costa Machado, Jorão Gomes Jr., Simon Razniewski, Axel Polleres, Markus Kroetzsch and Peter Patel-Schneider

sessions.description: Ontology matching is a key interoperability enabler for the Semantic Web, as well as a useful technique in some classical data integration tasks dealing with the semantic heterogeneity problem. It takes ontologies as input and determines as output an alignment, that is, a set of correspondences between the semantically related entities of those ontologies. These correspondences can be used for various tasks, such as ontology merging, data interlinking, query answering or navigation over knowledge graphs. Thus, matching ontologies enables the knowledge and data expressed with the matched ontologies to interoperate. The workshop has the following goals: 1) To bring together leaders from academia, industry and user institutions to assess how academic advances are addressing real-world requirements. The workshop will strive to improve academic awareness of industrial and final user needs, and therefore, direct research towards those needs. Simultaneously, the workshop will serve to inform industry and user representatives about existing research efforts that may meet their requirements. The workshop will also investigate how the ontology matching technology is going to evolve, especially with respect to data interlinking, process matching, web table and knowledge graph matching tasks. 2) To conduct an extensive and rigorous evaluation of ontology matching and instance matching approaches through the OAEI (Ontology Alignment Evaluation Initiative) 2026 campaign and 3) To examine similarities and differences from other, old, new and emerging, techniques and usages, such as process matching, web table matching or knowledge embeddings.
sessions.organizers: Ernesto Jiménez-Ruiz, Sven Hertling, Huanyu Li, Cassia Trojahn, Oktie Hassanzadeh, Pavel Shvaiko and Jérôme Euzenat

sessions.description: The Workshop on Ontology Design and Patterns (WOP) is an established venue for discussing best practices, reusable solutions, and methodological advances in ontology engineering. Now in its 17th edition, WOP continues to bring together researchers and practitioners interested in improving the quality, usability, and maintainability of ontologies through the use of design patterns and structured modeling approaches. Ontology Design Patterns (ODPs) capture reusable modeling solutions to recurring ontology engineering problems. They support ontology developers by providing guidance on modeling decisions, facilitating reuse, improving interoperability, and enabling more systematic knowledge representation. Over the years, WOP has served as a forum for presenting new patterns, methodologies for pattern discovery and application, tools supporting pattern-based ontology engineering, and empirical evaluations of their effectiveness. WOP 2026 aims to foster discussion around emerging challenges and opportunities in pattern-based ontology development, including applications in knowledge graphs, semantic technologies, and AI-driven knowledge engineering. The workshop encourages contributions from both theoretical and applied perspectives, as well as insights from real-world deployments. Through presentations and community exchange, WOP 2026 will continue to advance the role of ontology design patterns in high-quality knowledge engineering.

sessions.description: KGQA has a long tradition in the Semantic Web community, particularly under the Question Answering over Linked Data (QALD) moniker and challenge series. With the rise of LLMs, the performance of state-of-the-art systems has improved dramatically. However, benchmark datasets in the space exhibit well-known limitations due, for example, to the manual cost of creating parallel corpora of natural language questions and structured queries. To address this issue, QAWiki (https://qawiki.org) proposes a collaboratively-edited community resource of hand-crafted question-query pairs, focusing currently on English & Spanish questions answered over Wikidata's SPARQL query service. The motivation is two-fold: (1) to evaluate KGQA systems over a hand-crafted collection of multilingual question-query pairs over Wikidata, and (2) to build a community centered around QAWiki, to expand and improve it, and thus expand and improve the resources available for training and benchmarking of KGQA systems.

sessions.description: The rapid adoption of Large Language Models (LLMs) in data management and Web applications has created new opportunities for natural language access, reasoning, and decision support. However, concerns about reliability, hallucinations, bias, and lack of explainability limit their use in sensitive scenarios. Graph-based representations, such as knowledge graphs and property graphs, offer a promising approach to address these limitations by providing structured knowledge that can validate and explain LLM outputs. The Graph-Enhanced LLMs for Trustworthy Web Data Management (GLOW) workshop explores how graph and Semantic Web technologies can enhance the trustworthiness of LLM-driven data management systems. In particular, it investigates graph-based retrieval and reasoning, ontology-guided modeling, and constraints that support more transparent and accountable LLM-based Web applications. Now in its second edition, GLOW provides a dedicated space for research at the intersection of Semantic Web, Knowledge Graphs, and LLM-driven data-centric AI. The workshop builds on the success of its first edition, which attracted more than 20 submissions and resulted in a high-quality technical program.

sessions.description: The rapid increase in the adoption of knowledge graphs over the past years, both in the open data domain as well as the industry, means that data management solutions for knowledge graphs today have to support ever increasing amounts of data. The continously growing KGs resulting from the increasing popularity of semantic technologies highlight the necessity for scalable and efficient solutions for management of knowledge graphs in distributed, federated, and centralized environments. The DMKG workshop therefore invites novel research and advances in scalable data management solutions for large-scale knowledge graphs. Such data management solutions include techniques for storage and indexing, partitioning for decentralized/centralized systems, archiving and versioning, validation with SHACL/shEx, or federated data management. We welcome a broad range of papers including full research papers, vision papers, negative results, and system demonstrations. The main goal of the workshop is to bring together both early-stage and established researchers as well as industrial partners in order to facilitate communication and collaboration between partners in different domains on the issues relating to scalable data management techniques for large-scale knowledge graphs.

sessions.description: The purpose of this tutorial is to introduce the modeller to the notion of the good, the bad, and the ugly of representing knowledge in an ontology, reasons why they are not interchangeable, and provide theory, methods, and techniques to develop better ontologies. The overall goal is to equip the participant with more and more advanced foundations for developing ontologies and to provide hands-on experience, filling one’s engineering toolbox. Starting with some foundations of the representation languages and formalisation choices, the focus will be on evidence-based methods and techniques to find & fix issues, to prevent mistakes from entering in the ontology, and to improve on what has been represented even when it was not wrong. This involves methods that are logic-based and creatively use an automated reasoner to help modelling beyond pointing out inconsistencies or that are grounded in Ontology, such as operationalising the use of a foundational ontology, disentangling part-whole relations and features of object properties more broadly, and adding disjointness where they should be. Some systematised heuristics will pass the revue as well. This is an introductory tutorial at beginner and intermediate level of modelling.
sessions.organizers: C. Maria Keet
sessions.title: GOOD: GOod Ontologies and how to Develop them

sessions.description: OWL ontologies provide precise semantics and reliable reasoning capabilities and are widely used in many real-world domains, such as healthcare and finance. However, they face significant limitations in real-world applications, where knowledge is often incomplete or uncertain, which cannot be handled effectively by standard symbolic reasoning methods. In addition, building ontologies manually requires significant time and effort. Machine learning and Language Models (LMs) offer promising ways to tackle these problems. This tutorial, OntoLM, introduces the latest work at this intersection. It is a half-day program with two self-contained sessions: (1) Ontology embeddings, including geometric and LM-based embeddings, aim to encode logical and textual information into numerical representations for tasks such as ontology completion and inference. (2) Ontology reasoning and construction using embeddings and textual information leveraged by LMs. Topics include the use of LMs for OWL proof generation and abductive reasoning, ontology alignment with DeepOnto, and new concept placement. The tutorial combines lectures, worked examples, notebook-based resources, and interactive discussions. Participants will understand ontology embedding methods and how they can support ontology reasoning and construction alongside LMs.
sessions.organizers: Hui Yang, Jiaoyan Chen and Hang Dong
sessions.title: OntoLM: Ontology Embedding, Reasoning and Construction with Language Models

sessions.description: How can we build AI systems that do more than retrieve passages and generate plausible answers? In this tutorial, participants will build ARGO, a reproducible, open-source graph-based system for agentic semantic analysis across heterogeneous content. Starting from real documents and web pages, they will learn how to extract content and structure, identify entities and relations, retrieve relevant evidence, construct a semantic knowledge graph, and orchestrate reasoning through graph-based AI agents. ARGO connects core ideas from Semantic Web research with recent advances in information retrieval, Knowledge Graph engineering, GraphRAG, LLM-based tool calling, and MCP-enabled interoperability. Rather than treating retrieval, graph construction, reasoning, and validation as separate steps, the tutorial presents them as parts of a controllable agentic workflow. Agents decide when to search, when to inspect sources, when to traverse the graph, when to call tools, when to validate intermediate results, and when to generate a final answer. The result is not a simple chatbot, but a semantic AI system whose answers are grounded in source evidence, entities, relations, and explicit reasoning paths.
sessions.organizers: Ornella Vaccarelli, Federica Bove, Olivier D'Ancona, Anna Scius-Bertrand and Beat Wolf
sessions.title: ARGO: Agentic Retrieval and Graph Orchestration for Document Knowledge Systems

sessions.description: Knowledge Graph Embeddings (KGEs) provide fixed-length vector representations of entities and relations within a Knowledge Graph (KG), enabling a wide variety of downstream tasks over KGs. However, real-world KGs are dynamic, and continuously evolve with the addition of new entities, relations, and facts. Updating embeddings to reflect this growth without constantly retraining models from scratch, which is costly, presents a significant challenge. While generic continual learning approaches, such as fine-tuning, can be applied, they often fail to leverage the unique properties of KGs. Since late 2023, a new research direction, Continual Knowledge Graph Embedding (CKGE), has emerged to address this limitation. There is a growing interest in the field, with nearly twenty specialized methods proposed in recent years. This tutorial aims to first introduce the fundamentals and motivation behind KGEs, and then provide a comprehensive overview of CKGE. We present a structured categorization of state-of-the-art approaches, highlighting their underlying principles and differences, as well as the evaluation protocols and metrics specific to continual settings. In addition, we examine the problem of catastrophic forgetting, analyzing its causes in evolving KGs and its impact on model performance. The tutorial concludes by discussing open challenges and promising directions for future research in CKGE.
sessions.organizers: Gerard Pons and Anna Queralt
sessions.title: Continual Knowledge Graph Embedding: Foundations, Methods, and Open Challenges

sessions.description: This tutorial surveys major approaches for describing and validating different types of Knowledge Graphs, with particular attention to SHACL 1.2 and recent efforts to bridge RDF and Property Graph technologies. While RDF is the foundation of Semantic Web applications, Property Graphs are also widely used. Wikidata exemplifies the convergence of these approaches exporting RDF but incorporating Property Graph-like features such as qualifiers and references. RDF 1.2 further narrows this gap supporting statements about statements. Ensuring data quality in KGs requires validating data against predefined schemas or shapes. In the RDF ecosystem, ShEx and SHACL have been proposed for describing and validating data. More recently, SHACL 1.2 adds new expressive capabilities and alignment with RDF 1.2. For Property Graphs, some proposals like PGSchema, have emerged, while GQL introduces support for typed graphs and Wikidata complements its property constraint system with Entity Schemas based on ShEx.
sessions.organizers: Jose Emilio Labra Gayo
sessions.title: Shapes for Knowledge Graphs

sessions.description: Integrating heterogeneous data formats remains one of the most persistent obstacles in knowledge graph construction. Conventional approaches rely on dedicated mapping languages and separate toolchains, adding complexity that often falls to domain experts rather than engineers. Façade-X takes a different route: by exposing any format — CSV, JSON, XML, spreadsheets, and more — as a knowledge graph queryable with SPARQL alone, it removes the need for a second mapping language and keeps the entire workflow within familiar Semantic Web standards. This half-day tutorial introduces the Façade-X design philosophy and its underlying metamodel, then puts it into practice through a central hands-on session using SPARQL Anything, the reference open-source implementation. Participants query real non-RDF data directly with SPARQL, explore functions and magic properties, and work through guided exercises. The tutorial also brings in industry perspectives from production deployments, reflects on classroom teaching experience, and presents the standardisation roadmap of the W3C Façade-X Community Group. Pitched at an intermediate level, it targets knowledge graph engineers, data integration practitioners, Semantic Web researchers, and educators. Basic SPARQL familiarity is assumed; no prior knowledge of Façade-X is required.
sessions.organizers: Luigi Asprino, Enrico Daga, Martin van Harmelen, Ryan Shaw, Mathias Vanden Auweele and Ivo Velitchkov

sessions.description: The Knowledge Graphs and Neurosymbolic AI Systems (KG-NeSy) workshop aims to bring together researchers and practitioners who are actively working on combining KGs and Neurosymbolic AI, exploring how these two research areas can mutually enhance one another. In particular, the workshop addresses the following complementary strands of research: (1) KGs within Neurosymbolic (NeSy) AI systems, either as (a) deeply integrated components supporting hybrid reasoning, as (b) auxiliary structures improving explainability, interpretability, robustness, generalization, and transferability of deep learning models, or as (c) structured inputs enabling neurosymbolic prediction and inference. (2) NeSy AI to support KG engineering. Neurosymbolic AI approaches can assist in the Knowledge Graphs engineering lifecycle, e.g., ontology construction, entity and relation extraction, knowledge integration and mapping, completion via logical reasoning or validation, refinement via learning-based methods, and continuous evaluation and maintenance. Even when KGs are not explicitly embedded inside Neurosymbolic AI approaches, these approaches can improve methods and tools for knowledge engineering, paving the way for the next generation of Knowledge Graphs development practices. (3) KG-based approaches for understanding and systematizing NeSy AI, e.g., through design patterns, taxonomies, conceptual frameworks, or boxology representations. These works are crucial for identifying gaps in current approaches, aligning fragmented research landscapes, and opening up new opportunities for future developments.
sessions.organizers: Shqiponja Ahmetaj, Fajar J. Ekaputra, Sebastian Neumaier, Andreas Ekelhart and Cogan Shimizu
sessions.title: KG-NeSy: The Third Workshop on Knowledge Graphs and Neurosymbolic AI

sessions.description: Technological solutions are essential for effectively using data in research, but compatibility issues in scientific data can impede progress. Interoperability and data access are key, making the Semantic Web a valuable solution. The link between Semantic Web (SW) technologies and Materials Science and Engineering (MSE) goes back to before 2001, with the Plinius ontology from 1994 as a significant example. Recent conferences such as FEMS-Euromat and the MSE Congress show increasing interest in SW applications. Additionally, the EU has proposed a Materials Commons for better access to materials science data. This workshop aims to highlight the use of SW technologies in MSE and make them more accessible. We will provide an overview of existing approaches, connect stakeholders, and promote collaboration. By leveraging SW technologies in MSE, we aim to enhance research outcomes and foster a more connected research environment.

sessions.description: As knowledge grows faster than ever, transforming unstructured text into structured, machine-understandable knowledge remains a central challenge in AI. This challenge explores the next frontier of Ontology Learning (OL)—moving beyond isolated subtasks toward fully integrated, intelligent systems. Building upon LLMs4OL tasks paradigms, participants will tackle three visionary scenarios: building ontologies end-to-end from raw text, continuously extending existing knowledge structures, and learning taxonomies that generalize across domains. Together, these tasks reflect real-world demands where knowledge is dynamic, interconnected, and domain-spanning. Powered by the OntoLearner framework (https://ontolearner.readthedocs.io/), the challenge provides a unified environment for reproducible benchmarking, modular pipelines, and scalable evaluation. It invites researchers to push the limits of large language models in constructing, evolving, and transferring structured knowledge.

sessions.description: Mainstream Knowledge Graphs (KGs) often assume a monolithic notion of truth, offering limited support for context-dependent validity, conflicting viewpoints, knowledge evolution, and concept drift. This full-day Barstuhl workshop introduces emph{Multi-dimensional Knowledge Graphs (MKGs)} as an umbrella paradigm for contextual, perspectival, and temporal knowledge representation. It will bring together formal and engineering perspectives to examine key modelling formalisms, scalability challenges, and reference use cases through lightning pitches and collaborative breakouts. The main outcome will be a community-driven framework document that will serve as the foundation for an MKG white paper and a potential future Dagstuhl seminar.
sessions.title: Multi-dimensional Knowledge Graphs (MKG)

sessions.description: Data is the key to understanding and solving challenges such as the loss of biodiversity, predicting recurring weather phenomena, or the fragmentation and loss of context of our cultural heritage. For this, vast amounts of data from many different sources need to be interpreted. Due to advances in computer power and the increasing availability of data spanning longer periods of time, historical data is becoming more important to include. Unfortunately, many AI tools are not well-suited to deal with this type of data and integrating contemporary and historical data streams is a complex problem. In this workshop, we bring together computer scientists, digital humanities researchers, and cultural heritage professionals to create a whitepaper detailing the challenges for AI-assisted integration of heterogeneous and asynchronous data streams from contemporary and historical sources.

sessions.description: Transformer-based Large Language Models (Tb-LLMs) demonstrate extraordinary capabilities and, thus, change the approach of conducting research even in Knowledge Representation. Building on existing research that neural networks (NNs) on discrete symbols operate as holistic reasoners over “classical” symbolic approaches, this tutorial aims to present the dominant paradigm of Tb-LLMs according to the idea that these models can be understood with neuro-symbolic, ontology-grounded approaches and controlled through mechanistic interpretable or explainable KG reasoning methods. Offering a profound understanding of the inner workings of these models, the tutorial will help practitioners build novel, transparent architectures to model symbolic knowledge in NN.

sessions.title: Neural Networks meet Explicit Knowledge Representation: Towards Mechanistic Interpretability and Neuro-symbolic Modeling by-design

sessions.description: Abstract: This tutorial is the perfect mix of formal ontology meets practical application for use in modern information systems. This tutorial will introduce OWL reasoning while focusing on those constructs of OWL that Mark has personally found to be the most practical and useful in real-life information systems. Such practical reasoning is especially important in this resurgent AI era, where symbolic, semantic models can valuably augment LLMs with asserted and inferred facts to help avoid hallucinations while providing explainable reasoning. Goal: The goal of this tutorial is to teach key elements of OWL Reasoning, and how to execute reasoning in the Protégé Desktop tool. Expected Audience: Beginners to OWL Reasoning (or Beginners to using Protégé for OWL Reasoning). Background and Experience: Participants shouldn’t have to be too technical. Some familiarity with the idea of RDF may be helpful. However, being detail-oriented will be important! Also, they need competency and comfort with desktop tools so that they can follow directions and point and click and type in a bunch of stuff. Therefore, technologists are probably the main target (especially data modelers). However, technically minded businesspeople may also enjoy it. Computer science and Engineering students should fit right in!

sessions.description: RAGE-KG explores the state of the art and goes beyond in integrating Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) with Knowledge Graphs as well as the synergies between Large Language Models and the Linked Open Data ecosystem. We aim to foster innovative RAG architectures relying on Semantic Web standards and new approaches to make Linked Open Data usable by LLMs, enhancing their ability to generate reliable, verifiable and context-aware responses based on structured, decentralized and authoritative data sources. This year the workshop welcomes a special track on RAG-systems for Human-AI Value Alignment, seeking contribution on RAG-based approaches for content moderation and harm reduction and to deal with human subjectivity. The workshop will be a full-day event featuring keynotes, paper presentations, and lightning talks on emerging RAG trends (e.g., agentic RAG), along with a dedicated session on the evaluation of RAG technologies aimed at building a community of practice on this theme.

agenda.abstract: While it is difficult to formally define what they are precisely, Open Scholarly Infrastructures (OSIs) are a fundamental building block for the implementation of the Open Science goals as introduced by UNESCO, since they play roles in reforms, address critical gaps, and, more generally, enable more inclusive, equitable, and transparent science in all disciplines and academic communities. Even if the OSI community broadly agrees that the sum of their endeavours could surpass the outreach of proprietary systems, presenting such OSIs as a unique decentralised commodity requires first addressing one of the most crucial and delicate problems in information systems: interoperability. In this talk, I will introduce recent efforts from the past few years to provide standards and tools that support the implementation of interoperability, particularly at the technical and semantic levels, with a focus on the OSIs maintaining Scientific Knowledge Graphs (SKGs), which is one of the main topics of the Sci-K workshop series.

sessions.description: SWODCH 2026 is the sixth edition of the International Workshop on Semantic Web and Ontology Design for Cultural Heritage. The purpose of SWODCH is twofold. First, it aims to gather original research on foundational issues arising from the design of conceptual models, ontologies, and Semantic Web (SW) technologies for Cultural Heritage (CH) and the Digital Humanities (DH). The heterogeneous and multi-format data available in these domains call for principled methodologies and technologies to semantically characterise, integrate, and reason over data, as well as to support its retrieval, management, analysis, and visualisation. The workshop also welcomes studies addressing the philosophical and social analysis of CH and DH data and knowledge representation models, as ontologies in these domains often need to account for the historical and social dimensions of data. Second, SWODCH aims to bring together stakeholders – scholars from Computer Science and the Humanities and GLAM professionals, representatives from CH institutions, etc. – who are involved in the development and deployment of concrete SW solutions for Cultural Heritage. This includes solutions for building, managing, exploring, visualising, or mining concrete or virtual knowledge graphs. In this context, SW solutions should be designed in accordance with the FAIR principles and support the creation of CH datasets and applications that adhere to these standards.

sessions.description:
The AI Assistants for Knowledge Engineering (AIAA4KE) 2026 workshop explores the potential of generative AI and agentic workflows in Knowledge Engineering. While AI-assisted approaches have revolutionised general software engineering, knowledge engineering — including ontology modelling and knowledge graph (KG) construction — remains a bottleneck, reliant on scarce human expertise. AIAA4KE provides a platform to discuss topics such as multi-modal user intent analysis, automated ontology matching, and KG curation from diverse data sources. Key focus areas include developing evaluation benchmarks, integrating emerging standards like MCP-based agentic systems, and implementing human-in-the-loop governance for auditing AI-driven changes. We welcome presentations across the RDF/OWL and labelled property graph communities, aiming to scale knowledge engineering through robust, industry-ready AI assistants. AIAA4KE seeks to connect three key communities:
  • Research communities at the intersection of AI assistants and Semantic Web technologies focus on developing technically sound methods, but often lack opportunities to validate their work in real-world settings.
  • Industry practitioners are actively building AI assistants for ontology and KG creation, yet face challenges around the accessibility of Semantic Web technologies and the difficulty of evaluating the quality and alignment of generated outputs.
  • Standardisation experts, active in both academia and industry, are well-positioned to bridge these communities but are often underrepresented in the conversation.
By bringing these groups together, AIAA4KE aims to foster collaboration, accelerate innovation, and ensure that the combination of these technologies is both scientifically rigorous and practically applicable.

sessions.description: SemIIM 2026 focuses on advanced semantic information modelling, encompassing both foundational methods and large-scale industrial applications across data-intensive domains. With the rapid rise of digital twins and AI-driven operations, semantic modelling has become a critical enabler for structured, interoperable, and trustworthy data infrastructures. Across sectors such as manufacturing, energy, and high-tech systems, semantic technologies are increasingly deployed to support intelligent services, automation, and cross-system integration. The workshop aims to bridge academia and industry by bringing together researchers, practitioners, and technology leaders. It provides a platform for presenting theoretical advances, modelling methodologies, engineering tools, and industrial case studies demonstrating how semantic technologies generate measurable operational value and contribute to emerging data and interoperability standards. The program will feature invited keynotes and peer-reviewed contributions addressing the modelling of concepts, relationships, constraints, and operational rules for scalable data semantics. By connecting cutting-edge research with real-world deployments, SemIIM 2026 fosters dialogue on how semantic modelling can enable robust, explainable, and sustainable AI systems in complex industrial ecosystems.

sessions.description: This half-day tutorial introduces participants to the practical challenges of achieving data interoperability across heterogeneous sources and to the advantages of an approach based on knowledge graphs. Considering a practical scenario in the mobility domain (the integration of public transport data with open knowledge from Wikidata), participants will learn how knowledge graphs can support data harmonisation and fusion. The session combines a conceptual introduction with a guided hands-on exercise using Chimera, an open-source framework for building declarative and composable semantic data transformation pipelines. Participants will design and execute a complete data integration pipeline from ingestion of structured data to RDF lifting, SPARQL-based enrichment and construction, and RDF lowering using only YAML route definitions and declarative mapping templates. No programming experience is required.

sessions.description: The tutorial presents a mature ecosystem of open-source applications that have developed around the knowledge development platform VocBench, to encompass the entire semantic dataset lifecycle, up to publication. Targeting an audience with diverse levels of experience, the tutorial includes hands-on sessions where participants are guided through the core features of the applications. Attendees will receive an overview of VocBench’s manifold editing capabilities, covering OWL, SKOS(-XL), and OntoLex‑Lemon, and will then gain hands‑on experience developing ontologies, thesauri, and lexicons. They will also learn about advanced governance features such as change history and validation workflows. Attendees will further be introduced to the metadata model shared by the two main platforms of the ecosystem: VocBench (for collaborative editing) and ShowVoc (for publication), which combines diverse vocabularies (DCAT, VoID, LIME) to support the management of multiple versions of RDF datasets, both locally hosted and published on the Web. They will apply this knowledge when deploying datasets on ShowVoc as a publication platform. Attendees will then practice managing multiple dataset versions, creating forks and branches to enable development alongside the mainline, and generating distributions. The tutorial will continue with a run‑through of additional features, ranging from validation through ICV and SHACL, bulk ingestion of tabular data with Sheet2RDF, and the use of custom forms and views. Finally, attendees will be given an overview of SELEN, which brings semantic‑elicitation capabilities designed to streamline both editing workflows and the exploitation of semantic datasets.
sessions.organizers: Manuel Fiorelli and Armando Stellato
sessions.title: VocBench & Co.: Encompassing the Full Data Lifecycle

sessions.description:
Legal automation requires not only the ability to represent legal texts in structured formats but also to capture their normative meaning in a way that supports automated reasoning. This tutorial focuses on two key standards Akoma Ntoso for the semantic representation of legal documents and LegalRuleML for modelling legal rules and norms—to enable end-to-end legal automation.

Participants will learn how to transform unstructured legal texts into richly annotated, machine-readable documents using Akoma Ntoso, and how to express obligations, permissions, prohibitions, and exceptions using LegalRuleML. The tutorial will demonstrate how these knowledge based technologies can be combined to build automated compliance systems, support legal reasoning, and deliver explainable outcomes. Real-world use cases from regulatory compliance and policy-driven systems will illustrate how these standards bridge the gap between legal drafting and executable models.
sessions.organizers: Generoso Longo, Guido Governatori and Monica Palmirani
sessions.title: Unlocking Legal Automation with Semantic Web Technology (ULA-SWeT)

sessions.description: Property graphs and RDF knowledge graphs are reaching a scale where processing them on a single machine is no longer practical, making graph partitioning an essential component for enabling distributed storage, querying, and analytics. Traditional partitioning methods, however, mainly focus on graph topology and often overlook the semantic information embedded in labels, entity types, schemas, and ontological constraints. This half-day tutorial explores semantic-aware partitioning of property graphs, focusing on approaches that leverage structural and semantic information to create partitions with improved query locality and reduced communication overhead across distributed systems. The tutorial first introduces the fundamentals of graph partitioning, including edge-cut, vertex-cut, and streaming-based methods, together with the main characteristics of property graphs and RDF knowledge graphs. It then discusses how semantic information can influence partitioning strategies and how these techniques can be integrated with modern distributed graph databases and query processing frameworks. Throughout the tutorial lectures, participants will be introduced to semantic-aware partitioning approaches for real-world knowledge graphs and will gain insights into their behavior compared with traditional semantics-agnostic techniques. The tutorial is aimed at researchers and practitioners in the Semantic Web and Knowledge Graph communities who are interested in scalable graph data management. No advanced background is required beyond basic familiarity with RDF or property graphs. By the end of the tutorial, participants will gain an overview of current research directions, practical experience with relevant tools, and insights into open challenges at the intersection of semantics and distributed graph processing.
sessions.organizers: Elisjana Ymeralli, Georgia Troullinou, Stefania Dumbrava and Haridimos Kondylakis
sessions.title: Semantic-Aware Partitioning of Property Graphs

sessions.description: Personalized recommendation systems increasingly influence how users discover information, products, services, and opportunities. However, contemporary recommendation approaches often rely on centralized user profiling and opaque machine learning pipelines that limit transparency, user agency, and privacy. Personal Knowledge Graphs (PKGs) provide a Semantic Web-native approach to representing user preferences, behaviors, context, and provenance, enabling recommendation systems that are explainable, interoperable, and user-centric. Recent advances in KG retrieval, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), federated learning (FL), and large language models (LLMs) have further expanded the possibilities of PKG-driven personalization. This tutorial introduces participants to the emerging area of PKG-powered recommendation systems. Participants will learn how PKGs can serve as semantic foundations for personalization, how decentralized learning architectures preserve user data sovereignty, how KG retrieval can support explainable recommendations, and how LLM-based recommendation systems can be grounded using personal and external KGs. The tutorial combines conceptual presentations with extensive hands-on activities using open-source notebooks, datasets, and software. Participants will construct PKGs, build recommendation pipelines, perform KG retrieval, and explore approaches for mitigating over-personalization and filter bubbles.
sessions.organizers: Oshani Seneviratne and Fernando Spadea
sessions.title: Personal Knowledge Graphs for LLM-Powered Decentralized Recommendations

sessions.description: In recent years, the synergy between eXplainable AI (XAI) and Knowledge Graphs (KGs) has gained momentum as an essential approach for achieving trust and improving understanding in AI systems. KGs provide structured and interconnected representations of (domain-specific) knowledge, XAI aims to provide insight for predicted results and/or to clarify how numeric machine/deep learning models function internally. By leveraging KGs within XAI, research can enhance the understanding and interpretability of AI models, making it easier for users to trust AI predictions. KGs can offer insights into the relationships and logic that AI systems use to reach conclusions. This can be particularly valuable in fields requiring high levels of transparency, such as healthcare, finance, and law, where understanding the rationale behind AI predictions and actions is crucial. Conversely, XAI can assist in constructing and refining KGs, helping to identify which aspects of KGs contribute most to accurate, reliable suggestions/conclusions. This workshop aims to bring together researchers, practitioners, and industry experts to explore challenges and opportunities of combining XAI with KGs, discussing novel methodologies, applications, and case studies. Contributions will span theoretical advances, practical tools, and industry applications.

sessions.description: The 4th Workshop on Evaluation of Language Models in Knowledge Engineering (ELMKE), co-located with ISWC 2026, focuses on advancing how language models (LMs) are assessed within knowledge engineering (KE). As LMs increasingly support tasks such as knowledge extraction, completion, and generation, robust and standardised evaluation remains a key challenge. Current approaches are often fragmented, heavily reliant on human judgement, and lack reproducibility, making it difficult to compare methods or build on prior work. ELMKE addresses this gap by fostering a community-driven effort to develop consistent, transparent, and scalable evaluation practices. The workshop brings together researchers and practitioners to share innovative methods, discuss limitations of existing approaches, and explore new paradigms for evaluating LM outputs. Particular attention is given to issues such as transparency, the role of human evaluation, and the broader implications of evaluation choices. In its fourth edition, ELMKE will feature presentations of recent research alongside interactive discussions aimed at shaping future directions. It also aims to encourage collaboration through the development of shared platforms, benchmarks, and dashboards, supporting long-term progress in reliable and reproducible evaluation for knowledge engineering.

sessions.description: This is a cross-over event aiming to stimulate the convergence between the communities focusing on Knowledge Graphs and those working on Model-driven Engineering of Information Systems. The initiative is motivated, among other factors, by the emerging notion of 'Context Graphs' highlighting the importance of traceable decision-making and process knowledge, something that has been traditionally captured through enterprise modeling languages and execution traces associated with the enterprise aspects described through such languages. The recent uptake of the Agentic AI paradigm, with renewed interest in workflow orchestration and contextualized delegation, further suggests a growing relevance of this convergence. The workshop aims to stimulate a two-way exchange of knowledge and technical enablers - how approaches commonly employed in Model-driven Engineering can support KG-based systems or processes; and vice versa, how enterprise modeling methods and diagrammatic model contents can be augmented by KGs and KG-based AI systems. Furthermore, we also look at KG-LLMs integration patterns that can benefit from model-driven engineering practices, towards novel knowledge-driven architectures and knowledge conversion modes.
sessions.organizers: Robert Andrei Buchmann, Dimitris Karagiannis and Dimitris Plexousakis

sessions.description: Knowledge Graphs (KGs) are increasingly relied upon as semantic infrastructure for AI systems — grounding generative models, supporting retrieval, and serving as machine-actionable memory for autonomous agents. These roles place new demands on KGs that traditional data quality (DQ) dimensions — accuracy, completeness, consistency, timeliness — only partially capture: what matters is no longer just whether facts are correct, but whether a KG’s semantics are sound enough for an AI system to depend on, including well-formed ontological commitments, correctly disambiguated entities and relations, traceable provenance, and machine-interpretable meaning. A KG can score well on conventional DQ metrics and still fail as AI infrastructure, since classical frameworks were designed for static, human-facing data rather than knowledge that machines interpret, traverse, and reason over. This Dagstuhl-style workshop argues that AI usage surfaces a new DQ landscape specific to KGs as semantic artifacts, distinct from DQ for AI in general, and brings together researchers and practitioners from the Semantic Web, Knowledge Graph, data management, and AI communities to identify the DQ dimensions distinctive to KGs in AI contexts and develop a shared research agenda going forward.
sessions.title: Rethinking Data Quality for Generative AI and Knowledge Graphs (ReDQ)

sessions.description: The emergence of LLM-based agentic AI has recreated many of the challenges formally faced by the Semantic Web Services (SWS) community two decades ago: how should agents with differing ontological commitments discover, compose, and invoke capabilities coherently? The original SWS response provided formally grounded capability descriptions and mechanisms for bridging ontological mismatches. Current agentic AI systems largely lack this formal rigour, reintroducing well-understood failure modes, such as a reliance on linguistic descriptions of services/tools/capabilities without enforcing semantic guarantees. Furthermore, the Multi-Agent Systems (MAS) community has developed rich models of agent-environment interaction through affordances, formalising what an agent can do given its current state and the environment it inhabits. This discussion-led workshop will re-examine the role of semantics within the description of agents and services, with a specific focus on the affordance frameworks that cut across the MAS, SWS, and Agentic AI communities. Through discussion, we will critically evaluate how this research, together with the use of the Semantic Web can inform the design of LLM-enabled agentic systems. The result will identify key challenges, open problems, and a shared research agenda for semantically grounded, interoperable agentic AI.
sessions.title: Semantic Affordances for the Web of Agents: Bridging Multi-Agent Systems, Semantic Web Services, and Agentic AI
